Issued at 130 PM CDT Fri Aug 14 2026

     THREAT FOR SIGNIFICANT FLASH FLOODING TONIGHT...

Early afternoon surface charts depict an elongated stationary 
front extending from central Virginia along the Ohio River 
northwestward toward Kansas City, Missouri. A series of mid- 
level perturbations are riding along and north as the front as 
evident by festering areas of showers and thunderstorms from 
Omaha, Nebraska to Indianapolis, Indiana. The western-most 
perturbation (near Omaha) is the strongest in the region, as 
demonstrated by broad anticyclonic upper-level venting depicted in
mid-level water vapor imagery as well as a clear cyclonic low- 
level circulation (a "warm-core" low) being sampled by both 
KOAX/KDMX WSR-88D radars. 

This evening, the Omaha warm-core low pressure system will 
shift eastward and encounter an increasingly unstable airmass 
(MUCAPE > 3000 J/kg) across southern Iowa. Rapid thunderstorm 
development and associated regions of latent heat release will 
be poised to intensify the warm core low west of the Mississippi
River by midnight, leading to augmented low-level moisture 
transport north of the stalled front and into the circulation. 
Intense moisture convergence will lead to unusually high 
tropical-like moisture values with mean PWATs forecasted to 
approach 2.5" (near all-time records per sounding climatology at
ILX/DVN) ahead of the low. Taken altogether, a cluster of 
thunderstorms with intense rain rates (3 to 5"/hr) is expected 
to develop and move into northern Illinois during the pre-dawn 
hours of Saturday morning. (This process is not unlike how 
tropical systems intensify and produce intense rain rates). 

While the center of the warm core low is expected to track more
or less along the I-88 or I-80 corridors during the morning 
hours, the west-to-east orientation axis of the instability axis
south of the core should promote the highest coverage of 
thunderstorms near and south of I-80. The thunderstorms are 
expected to reach the I-39 corridor sometime in the 1 to 3 AM 
timeframe, and then the I-55 and I-57 corridors sometime in the 
2 to 5 AM timeframe, and then northwestern Indiana after 5 AM. 
The back edge of thunderstorms would then work eastward through 
the area after daybreak, perhaps not clearing northwestern 
Indiana until the 10 AM to 1 PM timeframe. 

Owing to the repeated rounds of thunderstorms this past week, 
soils along and south of I-88 are saturated and prone to cause 
widespread flooding with as little as one half to one inch of 
rain. Even with the expectation for the warm-core low and 
associated region of heavy rain to be somewhat progressive 
tonight (moving quickly rather than staying over the same exact 
area), the intensity of rain rates should still nevertheless 
lead to a swath of 3 to 6 inches of rain (locally higher), as 
supported by 12Z HREF and REFS 24-hour LPMM QPF. Such rainfall 
over saturated soils would lead to widespread significant flash 
flooding including widespread road closures and even structure 
flooding. Accordingly, a rare Level 3 out of 4 flash flood 
threat has been issued by WPC for areas along and south of I- 80
(primarily along and south of a line from Mendota, Illinois to 
Fowler, Indiana). 

A Flood Watch for flash flooding has been issued across much of
northern Illinois in two segments. The first segment is along 
and south of I-80 and features heightened wording for 
significant flash flooding. The second segment is along the I-88
corridor for somewhat lower confidence flash flooding should 
the track of the warm core low and associated region of 
thunderstorms track further north than currently expected. Both 
segments will be in effect from 10 PM this evening through 10 AM
tomorrow. 

Not to be forgotten, cannot rule out locally damaging winds 
along the leading edge of the thunderstorm cluster tonight. Even
if winds do not technically meet severe criteria (58 mph), the 
saturated soils may allow for trees to fall easier than in 
typical conditions. At this point, currently see the threat for 
severe weather as secondary to the threat of flash flooding. 


Saturday Afternoon onward:

In the wake of the warm-core low, a few showers and areas of 
drizzle may linger as late as the afternoon. However, current 
thinking is that coverage should markedly decrease during the 
late morning and early afternoon hours. Attention then turns 
toward the next upper-level wave and an associated cold front 
due to sweep across the area late Saturday night into Sunday. Am
noting a trend toward less instability ahead of the front which
may limit the coverage of showers and storms across our area,
but it remains to be seen if such a trend will continue. So, will
maintain mid-range chance PoPs (30% or so) across the area 
through Sunday morning.
